title: ClinFusion: A Vision-Centric Multimodal LLM System for Holistic Medical Understanding
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) hold immense potential to revolutionize clinical practice, yet deploying them in the medical domain is fundamentally a vision-centric challenge: models must absorb knowledge from heterogeneous 2D and 3D medical images, and evaluation protocols must align with radiologists' clinical practice and provide an accurate, fine-grained and factualness-driven assessment. In this paper, we introduce ClinFusion, a vision-centric MLLM designed for holistic medical understanding that systematically addresses these limitations. We propose a compositional and cascaded vision encoder architecture featuring a Cascade Spatial-Aware Locality Fusion operator that unifies diverse 2D and native 3D medical image understanding within a fused encoder. We further introduce a vision-grounded evaluation framework, including MedIF-Bench for instruction-following assessment and a region-of-interest-grounded method for clinically aligned and factualness-driven report generation evaluation. We show that ClinFusion sets a new state-of-the-art across a comprehensive suite of 2D and 3D multimodal medical benchmarks---spanning visual question answering, report generation, and instruction following---as well as textual medical tasks, outperforming leading open-source medical MLLMs (\textit{e.g.}, Hulu-Med, Lingshu) on 20 out of 24 benchmarks and demonstrating multimodal capabilities better than powerful proprietary models such as GPT-5.2 and Gemini-3-Flash on 13 out of 16 benchmarks, and can be further augmented with agentic tool use for retrieval-augmented and tool-assisted clinical workflows. A blinded evaluation by board-certified radiologists confirms that ClinFusion produces the highest-ranked reports, and validates our RoI-grounded metric as achieving the strongest correlation with expert judgment among all automatic evaluation metrics examined.

title: GeneEmbedLLM: Harnessing Large Language Models for Gene Functional Embedding and Association Prediction
abstract: Effective and high-quality gene function representations are crucial for bioinformatics tasks. While biological knowledge about genes is inherently textual, encompassing functional descriptions and pathway annotations, current methods often rely on single-source, non-textual data, failing to capture the rich semantic information in multi-source gene annotations. In this paper, we propose GeneEmbedLLM, a Large Language Model (LLM)-powered framework for generating universal, semantically-aware gene embeddings. The proposed approach advances the gene representation learning through multi-source structured text integration from five authoritative databases and attribute-aware attention based on Longformer architecture and contrastive learning. Experimental results on diverse downstream tasks, ranging from molecular interactions and phenotypic dependencies to epigenetic regulation, confirm the validity and effectiveness of our proposed approach, where competitive performance is achieved across all evaluated benchmarks. We further validate the quality of the generated embeddings through comprehensive analyses, including embedding visualizations, intra-pathway similarity assessments, ablation study, and parameter analysis.

title: Multi-Agent Generative Artificial Intelligence for Transfusion Reaction Feature Extraction
abstract: BACKGROUND: Many transfusion reactions are not reported to hemovigilance systems, and the features needed to recognize them are often documented only in free-text clinical notes. We sought to develop and evaluate an open-source, multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline to extract transfusion reaction features defined by the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) Hemovigilance Module from clinical notes. METHODS: We curated 181 features from the NHSN protocol and developed a multi-stage pipeline that extracted features, their timing, and clinical details from free-text notes. Three open-weight large language models (Qwen 3.6-27B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Kimi K3) were applied to 50 notes from expert-written scenarios, published case reports, and MIMIC-IV discharge summaries. Two physicians independently evaluated every model output in a blinded interface. The primary analysis was restricted to feature occurrences with concordant physician assessments. RESULTS: Physicians agreed on 1,201 of 1,343 co-rated feature occurrences (89.4%; Krippendorff's alpha 0.73). Precision was above 0.98 for all models. Sensitivity was 0.774 (95% CI 0.745-0.800) for Kimi K3, 0.636 (0.604-0.667) for GPT-OSS-120B, and 0.624 (0.593-0.655) for Qwen 3.6-27B, and specificity ranged from 0.952 to 0.991. Omissions accounted for more than 94% of false negatives. Timing and clinical details were judged supported or reasonable in more than 92% and 97% of assessments, respectively. Results were consistent across note sources and in analyses including discordant assessments. CONCLUSION: Multi-agent AI pipelines provide a feasible method for extracting transfusion reaction signals from clinical notes with high precision. Our work may have applications in active hemovigilance, reaction classification, and big data research.

title: Benchmarking language models and agents for scientific reasoning in evolving materials laboratories
abstract: Large language models and the multi-agent systems built around them could accelerate materials discovery by connecting scientific knowledge with experimental decisions. Existing benchmarks establish capabilities in domain knowledge, multimodal interpretation and scientific tool use. As language models increasingly support materials research workflows, their ability to distinguish closely related material states and reason accurately with quantitative evidence remains insufficiently evaluated. These abilities are essential for comparing material responses, assessing mechanisms and maintaining reliable judgements as experimental evidence accumulates. We introduce MatScope to evaluate three connected capabilities. M1 tests unaided, condition-specific reasoning through 200 tasks spanning ten research functions, using aluminium and high-entropy alloys as representative material systems. M2 tests agent-assisted transfer of related knowledge to unresolved materials questions. MatEvoBench-20 tests initial forecasts across scientific dependency chains and revisions of still-hidden responses as observations accumulate. Across eleven model deployments, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, given-input calculations and many physical explanations are handled well. Fine-grained response estimates, comparisons between similar states and quantitatively supported choices remain substantially weaker. Related literature improves selected estimates, while condition and baseline mismatches limit transfer. Progressive observations calibrate some downstream responses and destabilize earlier accurate predictions. MatScope establishes measurable targets for developing reliable scientific reasoning in future self-evolving materials laboratories and materials-aware world models.

title: PersonaDrive: Human-Style Retrieval-Augmented VLA Agents for Closed-Loop Driving Simulation
abstract: Closed-loop driving simulators mostly fill their environments with traffic agents that behave alike, whether they are rule-based or learned. Recent methods that control driving style learn it from labels inferred from existing driving recordings, from synthetic data generated to reflect each style, or from reward weights estimated by a large language model (LLM). All of these are indirect estimates of a style, not recordings of people who were instructed to drive in it. We introduce PersonaDrive, a vision-language-action (VLA) driving agent that takes its style from retrieved human demonstrations. The demonstrations come from a new dataset in which 15 participants drove CARLA routes on a driving simulator under conservative, neutral, and aggressive instructions. PersonaDrive trains a lightweight retrieval head on features from a frozen image encoder and on control signals over per-style databases, and fine-tunes one VLA backbone over the retrieved demonstrations. Switching style only means searching a different FAISS index, with no retraining. On the Bench2Drive benchmark without style conditioning, PersonaDrive improves the Driving Score by 4.6% over SimLingo and by 2.5% over HiP-AD, a gain that fine-tuning without retrieval does not reproduce. With style conditioning, PersonaDrive outperforms the strongest baseline, Drive My Way, in every style, with a Driving Score 6.7% to 11.6% higher. Its driving also follows the instruction, since average speed rises by 19.8% from the conservative to the aggressive style. Each traffic agent is evaluated individually as a driving policy. The dataset and model weights are available on the project page: https://pervasiveautonomylab.github.io/personadrive-landpage/.

title: SNAPRAG: Cost-Efficient Knowledge Extraction Attack on RAG Systems via Adversarial Perturbations
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems improve Large Language Model (LLM) responses by incorporating information from external knowledge bases. However, recent studies have shown that attackers can extract substantial portions of private knowledge bases from RAG systems through repeated querying. Yet, state-of-the-art extraction attacks either rely heavily on external LLMs to generate adversarial queries or require a large number of queries. In this paper, we propose SNAPRAG, a novel and cost-efficient attack for extracting RAG knowledge bases through adversarial perturbations. Our approach algorithmically generates adversarial queries without relying on external LLMs and allows for a strictly configurable query budget. In particular, SNAPRAG uses a discrete token-mutation algorithm to generate novel queries in a strict black-box setting. Our adaptive dissimilarity threshold calibration systematically forces queries into unexplored semantic regions of the target database, enabling extraction with fewer queries. Specifically, to extract half of the target knowledge base, our method requires up to 6.77$\times$ fewer queries than existing approaches. Furthermore, within a fixed query budget, our method recovers up to 96.9%, outperforming the closest approach by 7.7-19.9%. We further evaluate SNAPRAG against active defenses, where it remains the leading attack on four of five defended targets, achieving 50.7-96.3% extraction rate.

title: BioFirewall: A genome-writing-native governance layer for design-stage biosecurity screening of agentic AI
abstract: AI design tools now plan genome-scale edits, and agentic systems execute those plans with progressively less human oversight. Biosecurity controls are limited to two points: refusal guardrails at the foundation model and sequence-identity screening at the synthesiser. The design stage between them, where the plan is specified, is governed by recommendations, not by any deployed system. We present BioFirewall, a rule-governed middleware that intercepts a genome-writing plan and returns allow, flag-for-review, or refuse across five genome-writing-native hazard axes: cargo, locus, edit type, germline and scale, with cited evidence, a signed design passport, a tamper-evident audit log, and tiered access. On a de-circularised benchmark of safe proxies scored against independent oracles, a function-aware cargo classifier reached a true-positive rate of 0.72 (95% CI 0.43 to 0.89) at a false-positive rate of 1.105%, the nearest attainable to 1%, on a held-out split. Language-model judges did not reliably screen these sequences: their engagement depended heavily on sequence class, so a rate conditioned on engagement does not measure screening performance. Under prompt injection, the blocking verdicts of the open-weight judges tested flipped to allow, while the deterministic screen remained invariant. None of the 288 legitimate plans was refused, giving a 95% upper bound on the false-refuse rate of 0.0103 for the evaluated corpus under an independence assumption, or 0.632 treating the three plan templates as independent units. On a held-out gene set, the locus axis was enriched for drivers of in vivo insertional oncogenesis (AUROC 0.605; odds ratio 3.34), and a session monitor intercepted the cross-call decomposition attacks it was built to detect. These results show design-stage governance is achievable within the evaluated scope. BioFirewall is open source under a permissive licence.

title: GPCRAgent: an intelligent multi-agent platform integrating knowledge graphs and large language models for GPCR-targeted drug discovery.
abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are major therapeutic targets in drug discovery. However, systematic characterization of GPCR functions and ligand interactions remains constrained by the high cost and complexity of experimental approaches. Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance in biomedical question answering, their direct application to GPCR research is limited by insufficient integration of structured domain knowledge and poor interpretability of generated inferences. This study aimed to develop an interpretable artificial intelligence framework for automated and traceable analysis of complex GPCR-related problems, and to evaluate its utility in GPCR knowledge reasoning, structural property interpretation, disease target prioritization and ligand recommendation. We developed GPCRAgent, a multi-agent artificial intelligence framework enabled by VecKG-CoReason, which integrates vector-based semantic retrieval with knowledge graph-guided collaborative reasoning. GPCRAgent was evaluated on benchmark tasks covering GPCR knowledge question answering, multiple-choice reasoning and structural property interpretation. Its practical utility was further assessed in an idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis case study, in which prioritized targets and ligand candidates were supported by molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations. GPCRAgent achieved accuracies of 85 % in GPCR knowledge question answering, 90 % in multiple-choice reasoning and 83 % in structural property interpretation, outperforming general-purpose LLMs across benchmark tasks. In an idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis case study, GPCRAgent identified LPAR1 as the top candidate and prioritized potential ligands. In a separate renal fibrosis study, experimental evaluation of the optimized LPAR1 ligand in kidney organoids showed suppressed fibrosis-associated marker induction during IL-1β-induced fibrosis. These results illustrate how the platform integrates evidence for target prioritization and structure-based ligand assessment. To facilitate broader adoption, an online platform (https://cbcb.cdutcm.edu.cn/GPCRAgent/) was developed to support GPCR-related drug discovery. By integrating structured knowledge retrieval with collaborative multi-agent reasoning, GPCRAgent provides an interpretable AI framework for evidence-based GPCR target prioritization, ligand recommendation, and decision support.

title: Event-Grounded Question Answering over Long Audio via Structured Retrieval
abstract: Answering natural-language questions over multi-hour audio requires reliable event recognition, temporal grounding, and efficient retrieval. We present LA-RAG (Long Audio Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a structured framework that converts audio into timestamped event records, stores them in an event database, and answers questions using intent-aware retrieval and LLM-based generation. LA-RAG supports two deployment settings: offline grounding mode, in which long recordings are pre-indexed for low-latency querying, and inference-time grounding mode, which performs query-conditioned grounding over shorter, open-ended clips. We evaluate LA-RAG on two synthetic 24-hour benchmarks, Home-IoT and Industrial-IoT, and on CASTELLA-QA and SpotSound-Bench-QA, which are QA versions of two public audio temporal grounding benchmarks that we construct. The results demonstrate effective long-audio question answering with low query-time latency after grounding and indexing. They also reveal a substantial gap between event detection and temporal localization in current large audio-language models. Explicit timestamped grounding consistently improves temporal localization while maintaining competitive detection accuracy. These findings establish structured grounding and retrieval as a practical complement to generative audio-language models for deployment-oriented long-audio understanding.

title: TrajWiki: Source-Grounded Memory Trajectories for Long-Horizon Dialogue Agents
abstract: Large language model agents have shown strong capabilities in generating coherent and contextually appropriate responses, yet robust long-horizon dialogue remains limited by the lack of external memory that is traceable, updatable, and diagnostically transparent. Existing memory-augmented agents often store memories as isolated records or overwritable states, making it difficult to preserve how information originates, evolves, conflicts, or becomes obsolete over time. We propose \textbf{TrajWiki}, a trajectory-based memory framework for long-horizon conversational agents. Instead of treating memory as static entries, TrajWiki represents each memory as a source-grounded evolution trajectory, maintained through immutable episodic snapshots and claim-level operations such as \texttt{ADD}, \texttt{REVISE}, and \texttt{DEPRECATE}. To reduce fragmentation and retrieval cost, TrajWiki further introduces \textbf{Memory Wiki}, a persistent intermediate layer that incrementally compiles dialogue history into structured and interlinked wiki pages capturing salient entities, events, quantities, topics, and conflicts. At inference time, queries are routed hierarchically from relevant wiki pages to linked memory trajectories, then to corresponding snapshots and source messages for evidence-grounded answer synthesis. Experiments on LoCoMo and MedMT show that TrajWiki improves long-horizon dialogue performance across both open-source and closed-source LLM backbones, while providing greater interpretability and diagnostic visibility into memory evolution, retrieval failures, and answer generation.

title: Science Edge Evaluation: SEE the Missing Step Toward Real Scientific Discovery
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly involved in scientific discovery, yet it remains unclear whether they can support complex real laboratory science. Here we introduce Science Edge Evaluation (SEE), a multimodal benchmark of expert-curated questions grounded in peer-reviewed literature and experimental practice in chemistry, biology, and materials science. Evaluation of 28 multimodal large language models (MLLMs) shows that even the best-performing model reaches only 54.9% accuracy. Moreover, general-purpose models outperform science-specialized models on average. In the visual-agent evaluation, the use of tools increases the best accuracy to 56.1%. Tool use can expand the information available to models, but more information does not necessarily lead to reliable scientific reasoning. The key challenge is whether models can manage tool-derived information within the boundaries of the original experimental evidence. Together, these findings reveal that current MLLMs still cannot reliably make justified and evidence-bounded inferences from experimental results, which is an essential capability in real scientific discovery. Bridging this gap requires MLLMs to transition from explaining established scientific concepts to deriving novel and evidence-based insights from experimental data.

title: HyPLM Technical Report
abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are standard tools for variant-effect prediction, protein annotation and design, but the compute needed to train and serve them keeps growing. We present HyPLM-Flash, an efficient and open PLM trained by Hyra 2.0, the research agent developed by our team. HyPLM-Flash is a 650-million-parameter masked language model trained on 726 billion tokens, 0.73 times the data of ESM-2 650M and a fifth to an eighth of the data of E1-600M and ESM C 600M. It runs on an inference engine with fused kernels and INT8 matrix multiplication, embedding about 130,000 residues per second on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU, 1.9 to 2.7 times faster than other 600M-class encoders. In a matched evaluation against 28 public checkpoints on 32 tasks, HyPLM-Flash reaches a ProteinGym zero-shot Spearman correlation of 0.409, statistically tied with ESM-2 650M, ESM C 600M and E1-600M, and the highest organismal-fitness score among self-supervised single-sequence models. It gives the best long-range contact precision of all models evaluated, including ESM-2 15B and ESM C 6B, and a lower masked-residue loss than ESM-2 650M, ESM C 600M and E1-600M on held-out sequences and on recently released PDB chains. Matching state-of-the-art accuracy at a fraction of the training and inference cost, HyPLM-Flash sets a new Pareto frontier for protein language models. We have released the model weights and the inference engine at https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/hyra-results/tree/main.

title: AOP-Smart-Finder: A High-Throughput Human-AI Hybrid Framework for AOP Discovery and Evidence Mapping from Large-Scale Literature
abstract: The rapid growth of scientific literature and the high heterogeneity of biological terminology and mechanistic descriptions make it difficult for researchers to integrate scattered research evidence, identify connections among biological events, and construct mechanistic networks. Here, we developed a high-throughput human-AI hybrid framework, AOP-Smart-Finder, for biological event discovery, relationship mining, and Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP) construction and evidence mapping from large-scale literature. This framework integrates Large Language Models (LLMs), AOP-Smart retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) technology, and Python-based automation, supporting two analysis modes: one based on a single compound and the other based on a predefined set of biological events. In the di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) case, the system processed 12,983 articles within 30 min and included 1,093 of them, from which it extracted 1,589 biological events (including 458 official key events [KEs] and 1,131 candidate KEs) and 2,519 key event relationships (KERs). In the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) case, the system identified 55 stressors from 437 articles and extracted 278 biological events and 548 event relationships. Following manual curation and Weight of Evidence (WoE) evaluation, a mechanistic network comprising 16 KEs and 23 KERs was ultimately constructed. This framework can either use existing AOPs as knowledge guidance for mechanistic expansion and evidence supplementation, or discover novel event connections and construct mechanistic networks around user-specified research topics. It provides a high-throughput, traceable, human-AI hybrid methodology for complex biological mechanism elucidation and AOP discovery driven by large-scale literature.

title: Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System for ICU Discharge Risk Assessment
abstract: Unplanned 30-day intensive care unit (ICU) readmission is a critical benchmark for evaluating healthcare quality. Most predictive models assume readmission risk depends solely on a patient's individual pathophysiological state, ignoring hospital operational context and resource capacity. In practice, discharge decisions are dynamic trade-offs between patient stability and bed turnover pressures. To address this gap, we develop an Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) for ICU discharge risk assessment. The system combines multi-agent collaborative extraction with self-evolving retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to eliminate template noise from progress notes, while constructing departmental workload indicators alongside admission flow features, continuous vital signs, and sparse medical codes (ICD/DRG). Addressing severe class imbalance (about 10.5% readmissions) and alarm fatigue, we implement data normalization, class reweighting, and decision-threshold calibration. In 20 independent runs across 20,000 ICU stays from MIMIC-III, empirical findings demonstrate that: vital signs alone have limited predictive capacity under real-world class imbalance (PR-AUC of 0.1387 +/- 0.0086); directly concatenating raw text embeddings degrades decision tree performance (XGBoost and LightGBM PR-AUC drop to 0.3893 and 0.4030); whereas an end-to-end multimodal fine-tuning architecture (Transformer E2E FineTune) utilizing layer-wise parameter freezing and differential learning rates reverses text negative transfer, achieving the highest AUROC of 0.8288 +/- 0.0110, PR-AUC of 0.4373 +/- 0.0310, and F1-Score of 0.4757 +/- 0.0196. Operational indicators supply independent risk signals, laying an engineering foundation for high-utility clinical decision support tools.

title: OptiCover: A Scalable and Multi-Surface Framework for Cold-Start Visual Optimization under Semantic Constraints
abstract: Selecting an effective cover photo is a critical yet understudied problem in visual merchandising for e-commerce marketplaces. On Airbnb, hosts upload many photos depicting different rooms, amenities, and points of interest, but must manually choose a single static cover photo that is reused across heterogeneous product surfaces. This creates substantial challenges: over 90\% of listing photos have no engagement labels, leading to a severe cold-start regime; guest preferences vary across surfaces and search intents, and visually captivating photos may be semantically misaligned with the underlying listing. At Airbnb scale, this corresponds to hundreds of millions of photos and hundreds of thousands of new uploads per day. We propose \emph{OptiCover}, a scalable framework for cold-start visual optimization under semantic constraints and multi-surface engagement signals. The framework combines (i) a photo candidate generator that identifies candidate photos through various proxies, (ii) lightweight vision heads applied to frozen CLIP embeddings for large-scale semantic scoring, (iii) a cross-modal grounding validator based on a vision-language model (VLM) that enforces semantic representativeness, and (iv) an Exploration Logging Module (ELM) that orchestrates the collection of randomized engagement data across heterogeneous product surfaces and contextual search intents. We evaluate OptiCover through extensive offline studies and multiple online experiments across HomePage, and Search surfaces. OptiCover is now deployed in production and performs tens of millions of photo swaps daily. Online results show a 1.5\% engagement lift on the HomePage and a 0.35\% increase in bookers on Search, generating millions of dollars in incremental revenue. Our findings suggest that action-space shaping and semantic constraints are primary drivers of performance.

title: Zero-Shot VLA Adaptation with Retrieved Guidance
abstract: Pre-training large parametric "Vision-Language-Action" (VLA) models on large demonstration datasets has recently yielded promising results for general-purpose manipulation. However, these models still struggle under even small domain shifts relative to the training data, such as changes in camera viewpoint, background, object identity, or robot morphology. Motivated by the success of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in language models, we pursue retrieval to boost VLA performance. Specifically, we seek to leverage retrieval from domain-mismatched, "in-the-wild" demonstration datasets like DROID to guide a VLA's behavior in a new target domain. To achieve this, we introduce RAGu, which overcomes robotics-specific challenges for RAG: (1) It incorporates simple geometric calibration to transform source demonstrations into the target setup and reduce cross-domain differences. (2) It uses a coarse-to-fine retrieval strategy that selects, from a large pool of pre-warped candidates, the trajectory most compatible with the base VLA. (3) It guides the VLA's flow-matching inference procedure rather than seeking to retrain the base model or expand its limited context window. We evaluate RAGu across real-world, simulation, sim-to-real transfer, and cross-embodiment humanoid manipulation. We find it improves real-world VLA success rates from 20% to 80% and outperforms the closest-related baselines in sim. Project website: raguvla.github.io

title: Efficient VLA Inference via Retrieval-Based Speculation and Hardware Acceleration
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to understand and execute complex instructions, but their autoregressive (AR) action generation introduces significant latency on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Speculative decoding can accelerate AR-based inference by parallelizing action generation and verification; however, existing approaches rely on costly draft models, which are inefficient on edge platforms. In this paper, we propose Zora, a hardware-software co-design framework for accelerating AR-based VLA inference. Specifically, Zora introduces a lightweight retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without additional neural draft models. We further reduce batch verification overhead through a kinematics-guided action-acceptance strategy and a KV-cache-sharing attention mechanism. To address the retrieval overhead introduced by RAG-based drafting, we co-design dedicated hardware support, Zora core, to address the memory irregularity in RAG-based drafting. We evaluate Zora on four VLA models with the LIBERO benchmark. Zora retains comparable accuracy while achieving up to 3.4$\times$ speedup with software-only optimization and up to 7.6$\times$ speedup with hardware support over GPUs.

title: From Fluent Text to Ontology-Compatible Definitions: A Quality-Control Agentic Workflow
abstract: Biomedical ontologies are structured knowledge systems that must evolve continuously to represent newly emerging knowledge, but their manual maintenance remains time-consuming and laborintensive. Textual definitions are especially costly because they must be readable to humans and compatible with controlled entities, relations, and logical constraints. Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising way to assist ontology engineering tasks, including definition generation. However, textual plausibility does not guarantee knowledge-system compatibility. A generated definition may be fluent and close to a reference definition, yet still fail to ground its implied entities or violate ontology-level constraints. Directly inserting such definitions into ontology libraries may therefore introduce entity-level hallucinations and logical inconsistencies. To address this problem, we propose two structured-knowledge incompatibility metrics, Entity Error Rate (EER) and Logical Inconsistency Rate (LIR), to quantify entity grounding and logical consistency for LLM-generated ontology definitions. We further develop an agentic quality-control (QC) workflow that treats definition generation as an iterative process rather than a direct decoding step: it generates definitions, extracts axioms, checks entity existence and logical consistency, and uses the resulting diagnostics to drive repair loops. Comprehensive experiments on Disease Ontology, Uberon Ontology, and Uberon-ConstraintStress demonstrate that EER and LIR complement conventional reference-based metrics by evaluating whether generated content can be grounded and checked inside the target ontology. The workflow effectively decreases EER while maintaining strong conventional text-generation performance. LIR further exposes sparse ontology-level logical failures that are invisible to text similarity metrics, although their repair remains limited.

title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
abstract: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which Gemini 4 agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 2.55x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

title: Human medial frontal neurons represent integrated semantic content and sensory evidence to inform decision-making
abstract: Humans can reconfigure how they act on the world from a single verbal instruction. Central to this capacity is the ability to represent what an instruction specifies and to bring that content to bear on incoming sensory evidence. However, little is known about where in the human brain instruction content is encoded, how it combines with sensory evidence to produce a choice, and how this integration relates to behavior. Here, we characterized single-neuron and population responses recorded in the ventral temporal cortex, medial temporal lobe, medial frontal cortex and ventromedial prefrontal cortex of neurosurgical patients performing a verbal instruction task. On each trial, a written instruction specified which stimulus feature was relevant and whether the correct response was to choose or to reject the stimulus that best matched it, so that the same image pair required opposite responses under different instructions. Only medial frontal populations jointly encoded the instructed task, and the target feature, whereas ventral temporal populations encoded stimulus features along axes that generalized across instruction conditions. Choice representation emerged first in ventromedial prefrontal and then in medial frontal cortex during stimulus presentation, before a motor response could be prepared. Shuffling instruction content selectively degraded prediction of medial frontal population activity, whereas shuffling stimulus identity selectively degraded ventral temporal activity. To ask how these representations could be computed, we trained a vision-language model with separable visual and linguistic streams converging on a recurrent decision module to perform the same task. Its visual embeddings predicted held-out ventral temporal activity and its recurrent activations revealed a task solution space that predicted medial frontal activity, and the strength of this alignment tracked behavioral accuracy. These results identify a cortical hierarchy in which medial frontal circuitry represents the content of verbal goals and acts on a ventral temporal substrate whose representational axes remain stable, and indicate that functional hierarchies discovered in artificial networks can serve as predictive models of human neural circuitry.

title: Systematic Profiling of Encoder Architectures and Multimodal Embeddings in Protein Foundation Models Reveals Data Set-Driven Separability Regimes in Prediction of Allosteric and Orthosteric Binding Sites.
abstract: Allosteric regulation represents a fundamental mechanism of protein function, yet distinguishing allosteric from orthosteric protein-binding sites remains a persistent computational challenge. While multimodal protein foundation models offer the potential to integrate complementary biological signals, including sequence, structure, functional annotations, and conformational dynamics, their performance determinants in allosteric binding site detection remain poorly understood. We introduce a unified computational framework for profiling multimodal protein foundation models across distinct binding site separability regimes. Rather than evaluating models solely by predictive accuracy, the framework combines systematic modality embedding ablations, encoder architecture comparisons, and variance decomposition to characterize how evolutionary, structural, functional, and dynamical information contributes to allosteric site discrimination. Using the OneProt multimodal model, we evaluate two complementary levels of multimodal integration: (a) encoder architectures that differ in the modalities incorporated during pretraining and (b) downstream combinations of pocket, sequence, and text embeddings used for classification. To systematically probe the determinants of model performance, we benchmark these configurations across four assembled data sets of protein complexes representing a spectrum of biological complexity and a range of structural, dynamic, and evolutionary contexts for orthosteric and allosteric binding sites. Through comprehensive embedding ablations, encoder architecture comparisons, and variance decomposition, we demonstrate that model performance is governed primarily by intrinsic data set properties rather than architectural complexity, with data set identity accounting for 63.7% of explainable variance. Across the data sets examined, we identify substantial differences not only in overall separability but also in the information accessible from different pretrained representations. Single-modality controls show that high predictive performance does not necessarily imply reliance on the explicitly provided pocket representation: depending on data set composition, substantial discrimination can already be obtained from sequence- or text-based multimodal representations. Within-protein comparisons nevertheless demonstrate that pocket-containing representations retain binding site-specific discriminatory information when protein identity and the associated sequence and text representations are held constant. At the encoder level, structural and molecular dynamics encoders provide the greatest benefit in intermediate and high separability settings. Example-level analysis further shows that combining data sets can reshape which binding sites are preferentially recognized. These findings establish that the success of multimodal foundation models depends critically on alignment between available modalities and the biological signatures that distinguish regulatory classes in each data set.

title: Zero-Shot Protein-Ligand Binding Site Prediction from Protein Sequence and SMILES
abstract: Accurate identification of protein-ligand binding sites is critical for mechanistic biology and drug discovery, yet predictive performance varies substantially across ligand families and data-availability regimes. We present a systematic ligand-aware benchmark and evaluation framework for residue-level binding-site prediction across three settings: overrepresented ligands with abundant examples, underrepresented ligands with limited examples, and zero-shot ligands unseen during training. Using a BioLiP2-derived dataset with ligand-specific sequence clustering, we evaluate a progressive three-stage sequence-based modeling suite designed to study these regimes. Stage 1 trains ligand-specific predictors using a pretrained protein language model (PLM). Stage 2 introduces ligand conditioning through learned embeddings, enabling a single multi-ligand model. Stage 3 replaces these embeddings with representations from a pretrained chemical language model (CLM) operating on SMILES, enabling prediction for previously unseen ligands. In the original three-stage comparison, Stage 2 achieved a higher ligand-macro F1 than Stage 1 on the overrepresented test set (0.5832 versus 0.4769), although the comparison simultaneously changes predictor architecture, ligand conditioning, and the training regime. Stage 2 also outperformed several sequence- and structure-based baselines. Stage 3 achieves a pooled residue-level F1 of 0.3109 and a ligand-macro F1 of 0.2338 on previously unseen ligands, while remaining competitive on represented ligands. Control experiments using constant, mismatched, and scrambled SMILES inputs reduce performance across all three test regimes, providing evidence that the model uses information associated with the supplied ligand input rather than relying solely on generic protein binding-site propensity. Ablations across five PLM scales and multiple CLMs further show that increasing PLM scale generally improves performance, although the trend is not strictly monotonic, whereas CLM scaling produces smaller and less consistent gains. Overall, this study provides a systematic benchmark for quantifying the effect of ligand data availability on residue-level binding-site prediction and for evaluating generalization to previously unseen ligands.

title: Multimodal AI in Oral Cancer: A PRISMA-Guided Systematic Review.
abstract: Oral cancer presents significant diagnostic and prognostic challenges, often due to late-stage detection and tumour heterogeneity. Recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL) and machine learning (ML), offer promising solutions by integrating multimodal biomedical data. This PRISMA-guided systematic review evaluates over 82 studies from 2015 to 2025 that apply convolutional neural networks, transformers and graph neural networks to oral cancer, using combinations of histopathology, radiology, genomics and clinical data. Results indicate that multimodal AI models consistently outperform unimodal approaches in diagnostic accuracy, AUC and survival prediction. Architectures employing attention mechanisms, graph embedding and fusion transformers demonstrate superior performance in tasks such as early lesion detection and treatment outcome modelling. Despite these advances, challenges persist in generalisability, data standardisation and clinical validation. Multimodal AI thus represents a paradigm shift toward precision oncology in oral cancer, warranting further research focused on interpretability, prospective validation and ethical clinical deployment.

title: IntentLens: Grounding Underspecified Multimodal Queries for Recommendation via Tool-Augmented Reasoning
abstract: As intelligent personal assistants are increasingly deployed in real-world scenarios, recommendation paradigms are shifting from passive preference matching to inferring user intent from underspecified multimodal inputs. In practical interactions, users typically issue a reference image paired with a vague natural language query, keeping key visual attributes, personalized preferences, and item-side constraints implicit. Existing recommendation methods either leverage historical user interactions augmented with multimodal item features or assume fully articulated textual queries; both paradigms struggle to resolve underspecified multimodal queries for accurate item matching. To address this limitation, we propose IntentLens, a tool-augmented recommendation framework that grounds ambiguous multimodal queries into query-relevant evidence prior to user-item matching. IntentLens follows a ground-then-rank pipeline: a shared multimodal LLM leverages visual tools, user memory modules, and item attribute retrieval tools to (i) infer latent user intent from image-text inputs and (ii) augment each candidate item with fine-grained, query-conditioned evidence. Subsequently, a lightweight ranker scores candidates based on the grounded representations. To facilitate research in this novel setting, we construct two benchmarks with underspecified multimodal queries, namely \textsc{GoogleReview-MMTool} and \textsc{Yelp-MMTool}. Extensive experiments on these benchmarks demonstrate that IntentLens outperforms competitive MLLM and retrieval baselines, and exhibits strong generalization to unseen categories and datasets.

title: When Are Multimodal Predictions Biologically Supported? A Diagnostic Evaluation Framework
abstract: Multimodal models in oncology can produce accurate predictions, but accurate prediction does not reveal whether the model has learned biology that is shared across modalities, biology confined to one modality, or spurious correlations that reflect confounders rather than genuine biology. We introduce DECAT, a model-agnostic post-hoc evaluation framework that classifies multimodal representations into four diagnostic scenarios (shared, spurious, modality-specific, or no signal) for a given task and modality, using five null-referenced metrics and a rule-based decision procedure. The framework operates on learned representations, requires no knowledge of which specific confounder is present, and returns indeterminate when the evidence is insufficient. We evaluate multimodal architecture properties using DECAT on synthetic data across four multimodal model classes spanning over 2,500 trained representations, and demonstrate its operational use on 8,979 TCGA patients with both multimodal model embeddings and five pretrained pathology foundation models. Entangled models (e.g., CLIP) detect shared signal near-perfectly on synthetic data but also falsely claim it when it is absent, doing so in the majority of such cases on real foundation model embeddings. This false claim rate increases with signal strength and sample size, so that larger cohorts and stronger representations produce more confident but still incorrect diagnoses. Applied to both multimodal TCGA embeddings and five pathology foundation models without paired RNA, DECAT detects confounding invisible to AUROC without requiring the confounder labels, as confirmed by post-hoc stratification.

title: Memory-Efficient Active Perception for Embodied Question Answering in Dynamic Human-Populated Scenes
abstract: Embodied Question Answering (EQA) couples active visual perception, vision-language reasoning, and sequential decision making, and has traditionally been evaluated in temporally stable environments where visual evidence can be accumulated reliably. In realistic multimedia settings such as dynamic human-populated scenes, however, moving people and transient occlusions introduce human-induced perceptual variations: task-relevant multimodal cues become transient, viewpoint-dependent, and incompletely captured in individual views. Conventional store-then-retrieve strategies generate redundant visual evidence and incur high inference cost, making them ill-suited to such variations. This exposes two core problems for embodied agents: resolving viewpoint-dependent ambiguity, and maintaining compact evidence for efficient inference. To address these challenges, we present DIVRR (Dynamic-Informed View Refinement with Relevance-guided Rotation and adaptive memory selection), a training-free active evidence-acquisition framework for EQA. DIVRR combines question-conditioned room guidance with relevance-triggered view augmentation to guide exploration and additional observation. Selective memory admission uses the same relevance signal as view augmentation to retain high-scoring evidence, reducing stored entries while keeping the retrieved visual context compact. To evaluate EQA under human-induced perceptual variations, we introduce DynHuman-EQA, a dynamic human-populated EQA dataset constructed in Habitat, comprising dynamic and static subsets under shared scene layouts. Experiments on DynHuman-EQA and HM-EQA show that DIVRR outperforms existing baselines in both accuracy and memory efficiency. The gains are most pronounced in dynamic human-populated scenes.

title: Learning Biological Hierarchies in Single-Cell Foundation Models
abstract: Cell types are organized by taxonomic relationships that define lineages in the so-called cell ontology. However, most existing foundation models typically ignore cell-type lineages encoded in this cell ontology. We introduce a biologically informed foundation model called scOntoFM, which embeds hierarchical cell ontology into representation learning. Using Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) distances from the ontology graph, our framework pairs efficient offline triplet sampling with hierarchical cell-ontology learning. This approach jointly preserves local neighborhoods and shapes the global embedding geometry to reflect the ontology structure. Across diverse cell- and gene-level benchmarks, the model consistently improves performance, with especially strong gains in zero-shot settings. Our model also balances batch integration with biological structure preservation, providing complementary perspectives to existing embedding evaluation frameworks and supporting scalable biological discovery.

title: MELD: Mutation Effect Learning through Differential embeddings
abstract: We introduce MELD (Mutation Effect Learning through Differential Embeddings), a compact model for predicting the functional consequences of single nucleotide variants (SNVs) by training directly on the wild-type (WT) versus mutant differential. Interpreting SNVs is central to clinical genomics, yet experimental characterization cannot scale to millions of observed variants. Leading sequence-to-function models (Enformer, Borzoi, AlphaGenome) are trained on absolute genomic tracks and score variants post hoc through in-silico mutagenesis (ISM), so the WT-mutant difference never enters the training loss. MELD instead places the logit difference {Delta}z = zmut - zwt inside the supervised objective. It combines a shared CNN-Transformer encoder, a mutant-specific mutation-mask boost, multiscale mutation-centered pooling, and a learned adaptive amplification factor . On ClinVar (1.57M variants), MELD (1.9M parameters) reached an AUROC of 0.986 versus 0.800 for a same-data, same-backbone ISM baseline, with ablations confirming the contribution of each component. On a shared benchmark, it outperformed frozen foundation models with 3-1,300x more parameters (AUROC 0.967 vs. 0.924 for AlphaGenome and 0.936 for Nucleotide Transformer). With only 50, 000 training variants, it exceeded the ISM baseline trained on all 1.48M (AUROC 0.903 vs. 0.796) variants. On BRCA1 saturation genome editing, frozen MELD achieved a Spearman {rho} of 0.42, above Borzoi (0.40), and ClinVar transfer raised it to 0.45. These results demonstrate that direct differential supervision is a compact, data-efficient alternative to post-hoc ISM scoring with substantially larger pretrained models.

title: SE-Diff: Simulator and Experience Enhanced Diffusion Model for Comprehensive ECG Generation
abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a leading cause of mortality worldwide. Electrocardiograms (ECGs) are the most widely used non-invasive tool for cardiac assessment, yet large, well-annotated ECG corpora are scarce due to cost, privacy, and workflow constraints. Generating ECGs can be beneficial for the mechanistic understanding of cardiac electrical activity, enable the construction of large, heterogeneous, and unbiased datasets, and facilitate privacy-preserving data sharing. Generating realistic ECG signals from clinical context is important yet underexplored. Recent work has leveraged diffusion models for text-to-ECG generation, but two challenges remain: (i) existing methods often overlook the physiological simulator knowledge of cardiac activity; and (ii) they ignore broader, experience-based clinical knowledge grounded in real-world practice. To address these gaps, we propose SE-Diff, a novel physiological simulator and experience enhanced diffusion model for comprehensive ECG generation. SE-Diff integrates a lightweight ordinary differential equation (ODE)-based ECG simulator into the diffusion process via a beat decoder and simulator-consistent constraints, injecting mechanistic priors that promote physiologically plausible waveforms. In parallel, we design an LLM-powered experience retrieval-augmented strategy to inject clinical knowledge, providing more guidance for ECG generation. Extensive experiments on real-world ECG datasets demonstrate that SE-Diff improves both signal fidelity and text-ECG semantic alignment over baselines, proving its superiority for text-to-ECG generation. We further show that the simulator-based and experience-based knowledge also benefit downstream ECG classification.

title: Blind Variation, Selective Retention: Improving Creative Idea Generation in AI Scientists
abstract: Scientific discovery requires ideas that are original, useful, and non-obvious. Yet AI scientists are typically given as much task information as possible during idea generation, which can anchor generation toward familiar approaches. Inspired by the cognitive framework of Blind Variation and Selective Retention (BVSR), we propose a discovery framework that separates these two roles of information: it generates proposals under deliberately limited task information to broaden exploration, then learns from proposals previously verified on the same task and their outcomes to retain promising candidates for costly empirical evaluation. We evaluate BVSR across five proposer models and 12 scientific tasks. Limiting task information substantially increases proposal originality and non-obviousness, and produces a larger share of highly creative and high-utility proposals than existing state-of-the-art prompting-based baselines. Learning from prior proposal outcomes on the task further improves candidate selection, discarding half of the candidates while retaining most top-performing proposals. When incorporated into existing AI-scientist workflows, BVSR achieves stronger discoveries across gene expression analysis, drug response prediction, anomaly detection, scaling law discovery, and brain activity prediction. These results suggest that effective AI scientists should use information differently across stages of discovery: constrain task-specific information during exploration while exploiting accumulated empirical experience on the task.

title: BharatSynthQA: A Context-Grounded Question Answering Dataset on Indian Temples and Religious Heritage
abstract: India's temples and other places of worship are among its richest repositories of cultural heritage, bringing together religious tradition, history, architecture, and art. Due to the widespread curiosity, people increasingly turn to Artificial Intelligence (AI) assistants for information about them. Current models are rarely trained or evaluated on this domain. We present BharatSynthQA, a passage grounded question answering (QA) dataset focused on Indian temples, which also covers other religious sites connected to them. Our pipeline crawls Wikipedia from topics seeded by authentic heritage sources, filters articles for topical relevance, and locations in India. Further it generates Boolean, factoid, and explanatory QA pairs with a fewshot prompted LLM. An LLM judge filters the pairs on answer correctness, retaining 98,677 of 131,494 generated pairs. Additionally, 300 human-annotated pairs are released separately as a reference set. Human evaluation of the subsample of this dataset showed 89.83% of the questions were formed correctly. Benchmarking five current LLMs shows that factoid token F1 is only 0.18-0.30 without the source passage but 0.73-0.77 with it, indicating that this domain is poorly captured in model knowledge. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/theshivam7/bharatsynth-qa to support research on culturally grounded QA and retrieval-augmented generation for Indian heritage.

title: Agents Propose, Code Verifies, Humans Decide: Verified Agentic Ingestion of Heterogeneous Scientific Tables into Relational Databases
abstract: Public scientific datasets rarely arrive analysis-ready. They arrive as messy folders of wide matrices, long tables, spreadsheets, and per-cohort files whose keys and encodings differ, and every reanalysis must reconnect them first. A coding agent can automate this, but its mistakes can look plausible, and without an audit trail, a mistake that corrupts data can go uncaught. We present an AI-assisted ingestion pipeline built on one rule: LLM agents propose, deterministic code verifies, and humans decide. Narrow agents see compact, citable evidence about the files, never the data, and return typed proposals. A verifier with 39 check types tests each proposal against that evidence in two loops, one for the schema's structure and one for its meaning, and a human reviewer approves the schema and the load. Code compiles PostgreSQL DDL, reshapes the data, quarantines rows it cannot place, records provenance, and reconciles every staged row against the database. On four public biomedical datasets, one held out from development, 9 of 20 first proposals failed a check and every failure was caught: the loops repaired eight, and a one-line reviewer edit fixed the ninth. All 45.1 million values loaded with zero reconciliation gap. Discovering a dataset's structure took 4-7 LLM calls and preparing its data at most one more, costing under $0.50 per dataset. In a separate test, each of nine planted data errors was quarantined with a reason or recorded in an audit log.

title: X-Talk: On the Underestimated Potential of Modular Speech-to-Speech Dialogue System
abstract: We present X-Talk, an open-source framework that champions a decoupled, modular design for LLM-driven speech-to-speech (S2S) systems. While the dominant trend favors end-to-end (E2E) modeling to optimize information flow, these "omni-models" often struggle to balance the competing objectives of complex speech tasks within a single network. X-Talk challenges this paradigm by demonstrating that a systematically optimized cascaded pipeline can achieve sub-second latency without sacrificing modular flexibility. Our framework seamlessly integrates specialized front-end components (e.g., VAD, speech enhancement) and diverse understanding models (e.g., ASR, emotion, and environmental sound analysis) with LLM capabilities like retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and tool use. By revitalizing the cascaded approach, X-Talk highlights the underestimated potential of modular S2S systems and provides a robust foundation for future research and applications.

title: StateRAG: Typed State Contracts for Complex Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Complex retrieval-augmented generation requires evidence retrieval and control over what to retrieve next, which paths to explore, whether evidence is sufficient, and which intermediate results to retain. Existing RAG paradigms encode these decisions through method-specific model contexts, traversal procedures, verification signals, and memory. We introduce StateRAG, which represents retrieval control as a typed state external to the final reader. The state records the query plan, typed traversal path, candidate evidence, verification verdict, and reusable artifacts, with defined field semantics and designated update sources. Ordered role operators propose field values, and the controller validates and commits accepted proposals. A one-time compact-evidence check may select Bypass. Otherwise, the controller combines the committed verdict with the remaining budget to select Release, Revise, or Fallback. The final reader is invoked only after a terminal action and at most once per query. Among the evaluated methods, StateRAG achieves the best score on 10 of 11 reported quality metrics across LongBench, QASPER, and DocVQA. Its LongBench macro-average EM and F1 exceed ReAct by 6.3 and 6.1 percentage points, and its largest task-level gain is 9.8 F1 points on MuSiQue. Under normalized model-size weighting, StateRAG records lower mean LLM-token use per query than ReAct across all five workloads. In a matched LongBench control, the typed, role-owned carrier exceeds a free-form shared carrier by 1.3, 2.2, and 3.0 percentage points in macro EM, F1, and accuracy, with 6.2% lower mean RET. Removing TAM, MARS, or SMP lowers every reported LongBench and QASPER ablation metric.

title: A Graph-Based Approach for Mapping Kernel-Level Telemetry to MITRE ATT&CK
abstract: Mapping observed system behavior to standardized frameworks such as MITRE ATT&CK is essential for threat-informed defense. Existing automated methods mostly depend on Cyber Threat Intelligence reports, which offer only retrospective accounts of attacks. Kernel-level telemetry, i.e., system calls, instead provides first-hand evidence of adversary behavior, but its volume and complexity have limited its use for automated mapping. Its content also makes it unsuitable for cloud-based analysis: command lines carry credentials, events carry user identifiers and network endpoints, and during an incident the telemetry reveals which defenses failed. In this work, we present Trace2ATT&CK, a framework that maps kernel-level telemetry to ATT&CK techniques entirely within the defender's infrastructure. Trace2ATT&CK collects events via eBPF, reconstructs the attacker's activity as a process-centric provenance graph, and condenses it into a compact execution graph. This graph is classified by locally deployed open-weight LLMs, using either pure prompting or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounded in the ATT&CK knowledge base, producing ranked technique candidates with supporting rationales. We evaluate Trace2ATT&CK on 347 Linux Atomic Red Team tests with seven open-weight LLMs. The best local configuration reaches an HR@5 of 66.57\% at the technique level. RAG improves over base prompting in every model and setting, by up to $+15.44$ percentage points, and the execution graph substantially outperforms raw telemetry while never exceeding the LLM context window. Finally, a frontier cloud model used as an upper-bound reference quantifies the cost of local inference at 24--28 percentage points. These results show that ATT&CK mapping from kernel-level telemetry is feasible without disclosing sensitive evidence to third-party services.

title: MMGraph-Agent: Agentic Multimodal RAG via Cache-Inspired Multimodal Knowledge HyperGraphs
abstract: Driven by increasingly complex real-world applications, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has evolved from textual pipelines to multimodal settings, comprising two complementary dimensions: knowledge organization and retrieval enhancement. However, existing methods still face challenges of high construction cost, context window limitations, and the lack of unified training across offline and online knowledge sources. To address these challenges, we propose MMGraph-Agent, a unified multimodal RAG framework based on cache-inspired multimodal knowledge hypergraphs. MMGraph-Agent enables extremely lightweight hypergraph construction with zero API cost and dynamic memory-based retrieval that alleviates long-context issues. Experiments across offline, online, and joint retrieval settings demonstrate consistent improvements in performance, efficiency, and architectural unification. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/MMGraph-Agent.

title: SciMARS: Multi-Agent Recursive Self-Improvement for Closed-Loop Scientific Discovery
abstract: We propose SciMARS, a framework for recursive task-local adaptation of multi-agent harnesses in closed-loop scientific discovery. Multi-agent systems coordinate analysis, experimental design, and verification as scientific evidence evolves. However, two problems limit their effectiveness: (i) without shared memory, agents lose observations and repeat work; (ii) fixed role procedures, handoffs, and memory policies perpetuate mistakes despite retained evidence. We address these problems with a shared evidence graph and separate component editors. SciMARS adapts roles and coordination; SciMARS + Memory adds a third editor for how agents record, retrieve, and receive evidence. Candidate probes guide composition and selection of the next harness. We evaluate scientific discovery through experimental-data replay and a digital twin. SciMARS + Memory resolves 12/18 GPT-6-Astra and 2/18 GLM-5.3 attempts on Autonomous Science Bench, compared with 8/18 and 1/18 for the base multi-agent team. On ScienceAgentBench and AppWorld, it solves 14/38 and 11/20 tasks, compared with 11/38 and 5/20 for the base team. These results support combining shared memory with harness adaptation across scientific and interactive tasks.

title: SpecXMaster Technical Report
abstract: Intelligent spectroscopy serves as a pivotal element in AI-driven closed-loop scientific discovery, functioning as the critical bridge between matter structure and artificial intelligence. However, conventional expert-dependent spectral interpretation encounters substantial hurdles, including susceptibility to human bias and error, dependence on limited specialized expertise, and variability across interpreters. To address these challenges, we propose SpecXMaster, an intelligent framework leveraging Agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL) for NMR molecular spectral interpretation. SpecXMaster enables automated extraction of multiplicity information from both 1H and 13C spectra directly from raw FID (free induction decay) data. This end-to-end pipeline enables fully automated interpretation of NMR spectra into chemical structures. It demonstrates superior performance across multiple public NMR interpretation benchmarks and has been refined through iterative evaluations by professional chemical spectroscopists. We believe that SpecXMaster, as a novel methodological paradigm for spectral interpretation, will have a profound impact on the organic chemistry community.

title: EvLink: Source-Grounded Evidence Linking for Graph RAG
abstract: Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) supports multi-hop reasoning by organizing corpora into structured graphs. However, graph reachability often captures semantic association rather than evidence support, so a reachable passage may still fail to justify a required cross-passage transition. We propose EvLink, an evidence-linking retriever that preserves passages as retrievable evidence units and builds evidence-supported transitions between them. EvLink constructs two types of reliable links: relation-grounded evidence links justified by explicit source relations, and endpoint-alignment links serving as sourcebounded fallbacks. For retrieval, we introduce a two-stage retrieval strategy. First, bounded breadth-first search over source-grounded evidence links recovers bridge passages missed by similarity-based methods. Then, evidenceneed mining with noisy-OR coverage refinement selects a compact, non-redundant evidence set satisfying distinct question facets. Experiments on three multi-hop and two simple QA benchmarks show EvLink consistently outperforms leading GraphRAG baselines with average gains of 2.4 R@5, 1.9 EM, and 2.4 F1

title: ARMOR: Adaptive Curriculum Meta-Learning for Noise-Robust RAG Reasoning
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems have demonstrated remarkable effectiveness in mitigating hallucinations by incorporating external knowledge. However, the retrieval process inevitably introduces noise, posing significant challenges to RAG robustness. Fundamentally, noise robustness is a composite competency encompassing noise identification, retrieval filtering, and robust reasoning. Unfortunately, existing methods often fail to capture this holistic nature, typically restricted to single-dimensional enhancements or hampered by noise-induced optimization interference. To address these limitations, we decompose RAG robustness into three sub-tasks: knowledge boundary perception, retrieval verification, and robust reasoning. Accordingly, we propose ARMOR, an Adaptive Curriculum Meta-Learning for Noise Robust RAG Reasoning. Inspired by the teaching process, ARMOR introduces an adaptive task scheduler as a teacher to curate training plans according to the absolute learning progress of RAG generators (Student). Distinct from GRPO, ARMOR utilizes inter-group advantage estimation during learning to effectively mitigate mode collapse caused by limited output spaces. Experiments on three complex reasoning datasets (2WikiMultiHopQA, MusiQue, and HotPotQA) indicate that ARMOR achieves synergistic improvements in retrieval noise robustness, significantly outperforming baselines in output quality.

title: StealthyPoison: Manipulating LLM Agent Behavior through Procedural Poisoning of Third-Party Skills
abstract: LLM agents increasingly retrieve third-party skills from public registries and follow their procedures to complete user tasks. This reliance allows attackers to manipulate agent behavior by poisoning the skills. However, overtly malicious instructions can provide explicit signals for detection. We present StealthyPoison, a stealthy procedural poisoning attack that corrupts a skill's decision-critical rules to induce incorrect task outcomes while preserving its advertised functionality and normal execution. Unlike prior knowledge corruption attacks that craft poisoned content for known target question-answer pairs, StealthyPoison constructs reusable poisoned procedures from a publicly available third-party skill, without access to actual user requests or their ground-truth answers. To make the poisoned procedure generalize to unseen requests, it first synthesizes requests from the target skill and executes its clean version using a surrogate agent to obtain pseudo-references. These references and surrogate execution feedback guide the iterative refinement of payloads that alter decision-critical rules. To increase the likelihood that the poisoned skill is retrieved and selected over benign alternatives, the attack augments the poisoned skill's retrieval metadata with independently generated request descriptions. We evaluate StealthyPoison on 566 eligible target skills and 5,244 requests against more than 26,000 registry entries. It improves top-1 poisoned-skill placement by 13.6% relative to both HotFlip and GCG. Constructed using feedback from a single surrogate model, the procedural poisoning payloads transfer effectively and without modification to three held-out victim models and achieve end-to-end attack success in a Claude Code workflow powered by Opus 4.8. The defense evaluation further shows that most of these payloads evade detection by both SkillSpector and GPT-5.4-mini.

title: Retrieve What's Missing: Coverage-Maximizing Retrieval for Consistent Long Video Generation
abstract: Long-horizon video generation is a key capability of video world models, yet maintaining geometric consistency remains challenging. Memory-augmented generative models address this by retrieving historical frames, but their effectiveness depends on two key design choices: what 3D-geometric evidence should represent past observations, and how memory frames should be selected from this evidence. Pose-based field-of-view overlap provides lightweight but coarse geometric evidence, while explicit 3D scene memories offer finer spatial information at the cost of geometry estimation, alignment, and incremental updates over long rollouts. We propose Coverage-Maximizing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (CovRAG), a depth-based memory retrieval framework that uses pretrained 3D priors to construct a target-view coverage map as lightweight 3D memory evidence. For frame selection, CovRAG maximizes residual coverage gain, iteratively retrieving frames that explain target-view regions not covered by the temporal context or previously selected memories. To improve scalability in long-video generation, we introduce sliding-window depth caching for efficient geometry estimation. Experiments on RealEstate10K and DL3DV10K show that CovRAG improves long-horizon geometric consistency over the evaluated memory-retrieval baselines while maintaining low retrieval latency.

title: PCG-RAG: Progressive Compositional Grounding for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Complex Web Question Answering
abstract: Complex Web question answering requires retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems to identify target entities from multi-clue descriptions and connect evidence scattered across long Web pages. Individual pages often support only some of the required semantic constraints, while clues discovered on one page guide subsequent searches on others. However, premature reliance on partially supported entity hypotheses can divert retrieval from the original information need. RAG systems must therefore use partial evidence to guide further searches while seeking the evidence needed to establish the intended entities. We propose PCG-RAG, a novel RAG framework based on Progressive Compositional Grounding (PCG). Progressive Evidence Acquisition directs subsequent searches toward missing evidence for candidate attributes and relations. Compositional Reasoning separates candidate-guided retrieval from evidence-based answering along a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of subquestions. Provisional names make dependent searches specific, while answering tasks use accepted results and unresolved identifying conditions, assessed against the original question. New passages connect the identifying clues to the requested relations, supporting evidence-based downstream answers. Evidence Grounding combines identifying and relational source passages with supported intermediate answers, connecting evidence across Web pages to the original conditions during final generation. On BrowseComp-Plus and WebWalkerQA, PCG-RAG improves accuracy over the leading compared baselines by 5.43 and 5.15 percentage points, respectively.

title: How Efficient Is Your Agent? Online Predictive Bounds under Budget Constraints
abstract: We evaluate AI agents in an online setting where tasks arrive sequentially and, before running each task, we construct an upper predictive bound on its \emph{time-to-success}---the number of interactions until the task is completed successfully. Under a limited budget, some runs are stopped early, so their time-to-success is unobserved (right-censored), and the correctness of the bound may be unknown. We introduce \emph{\textbf{PR}edictive Bounds for \textbf{O}nline \textbf{B}udget \textbf{E}fficiency} (\texttt{PROBE}), a method for constructing calibrated upper predictive bounds while adaptively allocating a limited budget across agent tasks to reduce the anticipated coverage deficit. Our method calibrates the bounds online using inverse-probability-weighted feedback together with a correction designed to minimize coverage deficit while remaining unbiased. We prove that \texttt{PROBE} provides a coverage guarantee for any finite time horizon while satisfying the budget constraint. Experiments on software engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, and instruction following show that \texttt{PROBE} attains a coverage rate closer to the target level with tighter predictive bounds than a calibrated baseline.
